THE IDEA TO KEEP
A breakout is a predefined crossing, not a promise. Confirmation and retests
trade additional information for changed timing and execution.
By the end of this chapter
• Determine when a fixed closing-breakout rule becomes observable.
• Separate signal recognition, an eligible entry, and a later failure.
• Reproduce the quantity, costs, and R result of a fully stated paper plan.
• Retain successful, failed, skipped, and ambiguous continuations in a review.
Builds on: The language of the market • Volume: participation behind price • Timeframes, sessions &
chart scales • Support, resistance & price areas • Classical chart patterns
A crossing needs a boundary and a clock
A breakout is a move beyond a previously identified price boundary or area. The word by itself
is incomplete: beyond which edge, by how much, using what price field, and at what
observation time? An intraday high above resistance and a completed close above it are
different conditions. Both are legitimate observations, but they define different events. A
downward crossing is often called a breakdown.
breakouts-answers-02.png:
Imagine Harbor has a resistance area from $49.70 to $50.00. A trade at $50.01 crosses the
upper edge, yet a rule requiring a close more than 1% above that edge needs a close above
$50.50. The small buffer is an illustrative convention, not an optimized or universally effective
threshold. Fix it beforehand. A level selected after seeing the crossing cannot fairly
demonstrate that you recognized a breakout in advance.
The exact price field changes the result
Suppose a fictional daily bar opens at $49.40, reaches $50.80, falls to $49.10, and closes at
$49.70. It crossed $50 intraday but did not finish above it. An intraday-break rule triggered; a
close-above-$50 rule did not; a close-above-$50.50 rule also did not. Describing the move as
false without naming the rule hides these differences. The label should refer to the event you
actually defined.
If you require the completed close, that information becomes available at the end of the
session. A backtest must then use a feasible subsequent execution convention, or an explicitly
justified closing-auction model with its actual order and information deadlines. It cannot
simply observe the finalized closing signal and assume a guaranteed trade at the same price.
The decision clock is part of the method. Treating timing as an afterthought can make a
historical breakout system appear better than it could have been.

Confirmation filters add requirements, not certainty
Some rules require a buffer, repeated closes, increased volume, or several conditions together.
These filters select a different set of observations and often delay recognition. They may
remove some failed moves and exclude some successful ones. Whether the tradeoff is useful
depends on measurement across the relevant universe and period. Calling a condition
confirmation does not confer statistical independence or proven effectiveness.
Consider an illustrative close above $50 with volume at least 1.5 times the prior twenty-session
mean. A $50.80 close on 1.6 times volume satisfies it. A $52 close on 1.2 times volume does
not, even if price keeps rising later. That exclusion is part of the rule rather than an error to
correct with hindsight. If you relax the volume requirement only on the examples that
subsequently succeed, you are changing the method after learning the outcome.
Retests are optional paths
After an upward crossing, price may revisit the former boundary; after a downward crossing, it
may revisit from below. Retest, pullback, and throwback terminology varies, so this book
describes the direction explicitly. A return toward the area is an observation. A supportive
reaction or renewed decline requires another defined condition. Price may also continue
without returning at all.
If Harbor closes at $51 beyond a $50 boundary, a retest rule might require a later low inside
$49.80-$50.20 followed by a close above $50.50 within three sessions. This original
convention makes the hypothesis testable. A low of $50.30 misses the specified visit, and a low
of $49 followed by a $49.50 close does not meet the supportive-close condition. Waiting can
improve the prospective entry price in some paths, miss others, or encounter an actual failure.
Record all three possibilities.
Execution can change the economics
Suppose the illustrative signal close is $50.80, a planned protective trigger is $48.80, and a
geometric reference is $54.80. At the signal price, nominal downside distance is $2 and upside
distance is $4. The next open is $52.20. Entering then changes those distances to $3.40 and
breakouts-answers-07.png:
$2.60, respectively. Their ratio changes from 2.0 to about 0.76. Neither calculation is an
expectancy because it supplies no probabilities or execution guarantees.
An overnight gap can also pass an intended order level entirely. A market order seeks execution
but does not guarantee the displayed price; a limit sets a price constraint but may not fill; a
stop-market order activates a market order when its trigger is reached. These distinctions
matter when a chart makes an entry look exact. A valid signal can lead to a poor executable
opportunity under the chosen plan, and declining that opportunity is consistent with having
recognized the chart event accurately.
Define failure without selecting the answer
A false-break definition needs a time window and a return condition. One illustrative rule calls
an upward closing breakout failed if any of the next three completed closes is below the original
$50 boundary. Another requires price to hit a protective trigger. They are different outcome
measures. Neither can label the event failed at the instant of the initial crossing; the later
observations have not happened yet.
A failed upward move does not automatically prove a profitable short trade. Reversing
direction introduces a new entry, costs, risk, and a hypothesis that can fail independently. Price
may oscillate across the area repeatedly. Study the full sequence instead of drawing arrows only
on the profitable sections. Breakout analysis becomes useful when it forces you to specify
boundaries, timing, execution, and update rules. Its value should be evaluated through that
complete process, not through a collection of memorable escape-from-the-range pictures.

Return to the main Harbor chart. Its session-9 close is $50.80 and session-10 close is $49.40.

condition in this main rule; the earlier volume-filter example is a separate comparison. Declare
failure if any of the next three completed closes is strictly below $50.00. Equality at either
threshold does not qualify. These arbitrary rules are supplied so two readers can classify the
same sequence without supplying missing decisions.

stop at $48.80 and a sell limit target at $54.80; if neither exits the position by the third post-

Read a retest with the future covered
Use a separate retest example to practice chronological interpretation. At the signal close of
$51, the fixed boundary is $50 and the visit area is $49.80-$50.20. Require a later low inside
that area and a close above $50.50 in the same session, within three sessions after the signal.
On the first later session, L50.30/C50.80 fails the visit condition. On the second,
L50.10/C50.60 meets both conditions; the event becomes known only at that second close. A
third session cannot be used to recognize it earlier.
Contrast two branches at that same second-session cutoff. L50.10/C50.40 visits but fails the
closing condition. L49.00/C50.60 fails this specific low-inside-area rule because the measured
low is outside it. The low and close do not prove that a trade occurred inside the area: eligible
transaction prices can jump over intervening values. A different rule based on any traded touch
needs the relevant transaction record or an explicit inference convention. State the field you
measured. These alternatives show why a rule must be read literally before its usefulness is
judged.
For a concrete counterexample, take two complete fictional eligible-price tapes. Tape A is 49.30
→ 49.00 → 50.60. Tape B is 49.30 → 49.00 → 50.00 → 50.60. Both have
049.30/H50.60/L49.00/C50.60; both fail the low-inside-$49.80-$50.20 rule. Only B
contains a traded touch at $50.00. A line drawn between A's $49.00 and $50.60 marks passes
across the area on paper, but that connecting stroke does not supply a transaction. Without the
tapes, their identical OHLC cannot distinguish the touch outcomes.

A WORKED EXAMPLE
A correct signal can end in a skip
At the session-9 close, $50.80 exceeds the frozen $50.50 threshold. At the session-10 open,
$52.20 exceeds the entry ceiling, so the paper plan skips. At the session-10 close, $49.40 is
below the $50 boundary and meets the failure definition. The three statements are compatible.
No position was opened, so neither a hypothetical stop loss nor the foregone target belongs in
realized P&L.
Pause & try it
Apply the supplied main Harbor rule at the session-9 close, session-10 open, and session-10
close. State the signal, entry decision, failure classification, and realized trade P&L at each
cutoff. For the target comparison branch, calculate entry notional and cash debit including entry
cost, planned price risk, cost-inclusive ordinary loss, and net target profit in dollars and R.
At the session-9 close, 50.80 > 50.50 establishes a signal; the next open and later failure are still
unknown. At the session-10 open, 52.20 > 50.80 requires a skip. At its close, 49.40 < 50.00
establishes failure inside the three-session window. There is no trade P&L, because there was no
entry; a skip is a retained opportunity record rather than a zero-R executed trade.
For the explicitly modeled $50.80 target branch: entry notional = 50 × $50.80 = $2,540; entry cash
debit = $2,542.50 including the $2.50 entry charge. Planned price risk = 50 x $2 = $100; ordinary
loss including $5 expense = $105. Target price profit = 50 x $4 = $200; net profit = $195; net R =
195/100 = +1.95R. The denominator is frozen filled-price risk, not notional or the $105 cost-inclusive
loss.
The comparison branches are invented continuations for inspecting the same plan. Their count is not
a sample of strategy success rates. A bar containing both exit prices would require the declared
ambiguity policy.

GUIDED PRACTICE
Follow the retest clock
Using the retest rule, classify day +1 L50.30/C50.80 and day +2 L50.10/C50.60. What changes if
day +2 closes at $50.40?
Day +1 misses the low-inside-$49.80-$50.20 condition. Day +2 meets the visit and close-
above-$50.50 conditions, recognized at its close. With C50.40, the visit occurs but the closing
condition fails; neither version licenses a day +1 recognition.
INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
A gap changes the realized loss
A comparison branch first models 50 shares bought at $50.80. The following session opens at
$47.80, below the $48.80 stop. Under the supplied gap rule and $5 expense, calculate the exit,
net P&L, and R. Explain why the ordinary $105 modeled loss is not the answer.
The gap rule exits at the assumed $47.80 open. Price loss = 50 × ($50.80 - $47.80) = $150; net P&L
= -$155; R = -155/100 = -1.55R. The trigger was skipped by the gap, so an exact $48.80 fill cannot
be assumed. The $105 figure described an ordinary exact-trigger exit, not a maximum possible loss.
INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Keep R tied to the eligible fill
A separate permitted branch opens at $50.40 and models the same 50-share entry, $48.80 stop,
$54.80 target and $5 round-trip charge. Calculate frozen 1R, entry cash debit, net target result
and net ordinary-stop result in dollars and R. How much of the maximum-entry cash reserve is
released?
The $50.40 opening entry is above $48.80 and at or below $50.80, so it is eligible. Frozen 1R = 50 x
($50.40 - $48.80) = $8o. Entry notional is $2,520; cash debit is $2,522.50. The $2,542.50
maximum-entry reserve releases $20.
breakouts-answers-14.png:
Target gross profit = 50 x $4.40 = $220; net = $215; net R = 215/80 = +2.6875R. Ordinary-stop net
loss = -$80 - $5 = -$85, 0r -1.0625R. Reusing the maximum-entry $100 denominator would
conceal the smaller filled-price risk.
INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
A traded touch needs a traded price
A different retest area is $72.80-$73.20 inclusive. For each complete fictional eligible-price tape
below, reconstruct OHLC and apply two rules: the completed low must be inside the area; or at
least one eligible trade must be inside it. Both rules additionally require a close strictly above
$73.50. Explain what an OHLC-only observer cannot distinguish.

CHECK YOUR UNDERSTANDING
One question before you go
At a $50.80 qualifying close, the plan permits only a next open at or below $50.80. The next open is
$52.20 and the close is $49.40. Which record follows the supplied rule?
A. Signal at the earlier close; buy at $50.80 because the later low passed it; stop loss.
B. Signal at the earlier close; skip at the open; chart failure at the later close.
C. No signal at the earlier close because the next close was below the boundary.
Answer: B. The opening-only policy skips, while signal recognition and later closing failure remain
distinct observations.

Confirmation filters add requirements, not certainty
Some rules require a buffer, repeated closes, increased volume, or several conditions together.
These filters select a different set of observations and often delay recognition. They may
remove some failed moves and exclude some successful ones. Whether the tradeoff is useful
depends on measurement across the relevant universe and period. Calling a condition
confirmation does not confer statistical independence or proven effectiveness.
Consider an illustrative close above $50 with volume at least 1.5 times the prior twenty-session
mean. A $50.80 close on 1.6 times volume satisfies it. A $52 close on 1.2 times volume does
not, even if price keeps rising later. That exclusion is part of the rule rather than an error to
correct with hindsight. If you relax the volume requirement only on the examples that
subsequently succeed, you are changing the method after learning the outcome.
Retests are optional paths
After an upward crossing, price may revisit the former boundary; after a downward crossing, it
may revisit from below. Retest, pullback, and throwback terminology varies, so this book
describes the direction explicitly. A return toward the area is an observation. A supportive
reaction or renewed decline requires another defined condition. Price may also continue
without returning at all.
If Harbor closes at $51 beyond a $50 boundary, a retest rule might require a later low inside
$49.80-$50.20 followed by a close above $50.50 within three sessions. This original
convention makes the hypothesis testable. A low of $50.30 misses the specified visit, and a low
of $49 followed by a $49.50 close does not meet the supportive-close condition. Waiting can
improve the prospective entry price in some paths, miss others, or encounter an actual failure.
Record all three possibilities.
Execution can change the economics
Suppose the illustrative signal close is $50.80, a planned protective trigger is $48.80, and a
geometric reference is $54.80. At the signal price, nominal downside distance is $2 and upside
distance is $4. The next open is $52.20. Entering then changes those distances to $3.40 and
breakouts-learner-07.png:
$2.60, respectively. Their ratio changes from 2.0 to about 0.76. Neither calculation is an
expectancy because it supplies no probabilities or execution guarantees.
An overnight gap can also pass an intended order level entirely. A market order seeks execution
but does not guarantee the displayed price; a limit sets a price constraint but may not fill; a
stop-market order activates a market order when its trigger is reached. These distinctions
matter when a chart makes an entry look exact. A valid signal can lead to a poor executable
opportunity under the chosen plan, and declining that opportunity is consistent with having
recognized the chart event accurately.
Define failure without selecting the answer
A false-break definition needs a time window and a return condition. One illustrative rule calls
an upward closing breakout failed if any of the next three completed closes is below the original
$50 boundary. Another requires price to hit a protective trigger. They are different outcome
measures. Neither can label the event failed at the instant of the initial crossing; the later
observations have not happened yet.
A failed upward move does not automatically prove a profitable short trade. Reversing
direction introduces a new entry, costs, risk, and a hypothesis that can fail independently. Price
may oscillate across the area repeatedly. Study the full sequence instead of drawing arrows only
on the profitable sections. Breakout analysis becomes useful when it forces you to specify
boundaries, timing, execution, and update rules. Its value should be evaluated through that
complete process, not through a collection of memorable escape-from-the-range pictures.

condition in this main rule; the earlier volume-filter example is a separate comparison. Declare
failure if any of the next three completed closes is strictly below $50.00. Equality at either
threshold does not qualify. These arbitrary rules are supplied so two readers can classify the
same sequence without supplying missing decisions.

application; they were not sampled from a real opportunity set. A count of winners in the
gallery would mostly measure the author's selection. Chapter 24 shows how a frozen research
rule and chronological evaluation window address a different question.

when an execution claim must stop; the calendar-selected archive gallery supplies small OHLC
windows with retrospective adjustments and undocumented session details. Apply the same
three-pass method: freeze the stated clock, identify missing inputs and distinguish later
classifications from the earlier decision. Neither documented market facts nor a systematically
recorded gallery turn a hypothetical fill into a historical transaction.

Historical case selection and data conventions
The historical cases below were selected to teach two data problems: an event-driven price
move and a share-unit change. Selection is purposive, based on publicly documented episodes,
rather than a random screen or an outcome-blind trading sample. Both the surge and
subsequent fall in the selected GME episode are included. These cases cannot estimate a hit
rate. Use the fictional cases earlier in the chapter to rehearse fully specified execution; these
historical records teach what can and cannot be inferred from limited observations.
Provenance: GME, January 12-28, 2021, is reconstructed from SEC statf report section 3.2,
printed pp. 18-19, published October 14, 2021. Prices use the dollar/share units reported for
that period, not a later split-adjusted chart. Reported closing prices are distinguished from
intraday highs; the report does not supply a complete OHLC series or exact timestamps for the
highs. No dividend reinvestment or price adjustment is performed here. Two closes are derived
from explicitly reported daily dollar changes, with the arithmetic disclosed in the table. Missing
sessions remain missing.
Reuse basis: the SEC's Webmaster FAQ states that Government-created site content is free to
access and reuse, while some content such as stock art is excluded. This book attributes a few
numeric facts from the staff report and makes its own table and diagram; it copies no vendor
chart, artwork or logo. The FAQ is not a license for a vendor's underlying market-data feed. The
Apple case paraphrases the issuer's dated announcement and uses original algebra, with no
copied chart or photo.
GME event reaction: a large move still leaves execution
unknown
At the January 13 close, compare the two completed closing observations and volumes shown
in the first panel. Price change is 31.40 - 19.95 = $11.45, or 57.39%; approximate share volume
is roughly 20 times the previous session (about 144 million against 7 million shares). These are
observations. The words "breakout" or "short squeeze" add an interpretation whose definition
and evidence must be supplied.

Apple's 2014 split: change the unit before classifying a
break
Apple announced a seven-for-one stock split on April 23, 2014, with a June 2 record date and
split-adjusted trading beginning June 9. This corporate-action case is selected to test unit
consistency, independently of any later return. The announcement is usable as an event-
calendar fact after its release; it supplies no entry or target prices.
At a June 6 analysis cutoff, the announced unit change belongs in the data plan for the next
session. If a pre-split price is P and volume is V, a consistently split-adjusted comparison
expresses that prior price as P/7 and prior share volume as 7V. A holder of N shares becomes a
holder of 7N shares, so NP = (7N)(P/7) before other price movement. P, V and N are algebraic
placeholders, not historical quotes. No dollar P&L is inferred. A raw discontinuity caused by
the share unit is not evidence of a structural support failure.
Decision record: request a daily feed with its adjustment convention and the corporate-action
flag before drawing a June 9 candle or computing a moving average across the date. The
supplied announcement alone leads to a data-check decision, not a trade. This makes "skip" a
completed analysis with a reason, rather than an empty chart opinion.
A calendar-selected historical gallery: freeze the
procedure first
The next gallery gives you a complete small OHLC window rather than a handful of famous-
event facts. Before downloading prices, we fixed three symbols-Apple (AAPL), Microsoft
(MSFT) and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) - and every month of 2016. The cutoff is the first
available archive session on or after each month's first day. Every one of the 36 symbol-month
cells stays in the ledger. The symbols and year are teaching choices, not a historical investable
universe; choosing familiar surviving securities introduces a selection limit even when dates
are chosen without looking at their outcomes.
The exercise gate is deliberately simple: compare the cutoff close C with the arithmetic mean of
the five preceding closes, excluding C. If C'is not strictly higher, record "skipped." If it is higher,
observe the next five archive sessions against an upper level of 1.01C and a lower level of 0.99C.
A session opening at or beyond a level resolves that side first. Otherwise compare its high and
low: a sole upper touch is "favorable," a sole lower touch "adverse," and touching both in that
first resolving bar is "ambiguous." No touch within five sessions is "ordinary/unresolved."
These labels describe a price path under an invented exercise rule. They are not successful or
failed historical trades.
case-studies-answers-17.png:
The full ledger below contains 18 skips, six favorable paths, eleven adverse paths and one
ordinary/unresolved path; none is an ambiguous first resolving bar. We show the earliest
example of each represented class, with alphabetical symbol order breaking date ties. This
representative choice is intentionally outcome-stratified, so the four illustrations are not a
sample from which to estimate probabilities. Do not divide favorable counts by eligible counts
to infer a strategy's success rate. There is no order, position, fill, stop execution, cash account,
commission model or held-out strategy test.
Provenance and reuse: Boris Marjanovic's Huge Stock Market Dataset on Kaggle, version 3,
provides the three daily files. Retrieved metadata explicitly declares CCo-1.0, and the depositor
states that prices are adjusted for dividends and splits. We copied numeric observations into
original tables and diagrams. The stated permission is the depositor's; metadata does not
identify an upstream provider or establish others' rights. The local source snapshots, exact
download URLs, SHA-256 hashes, extracts and frozen selection sheet are preserved in
data/historical/ for independent inspection.
Data conventions: source date labels and all OHLC decimals are retained, in the archive's
adjusted dollar scale. Daily aggregation is reported, but exact regular/extended-session
inclusion, time zone and adjustment formula are undocumented, and the adjustment vintage is
bounded only by the depositor's note "last updated 11/10/2017". We therefore call them archive
sessions, not certified regular-session candles. No missing date is interpolated. Volume is
unused because its adjustment convention is unspecified. These are retrospectively adjusted
records, not a reconstruction of prices published at each 2016 cutoff. The cutoff exercise hides
future bars; it does not make the adjusted vintage contemporaneous. Before modeling real
transactions, obtain documented raw quotes, corporate actions, precise sessions, spread and
order information.

A WORKED EXAMPLE
A fee convention changes the smaller gap's net R
GAPS, 30 shares: 1R $90, gross loss $300, costs $5, net -$305/-3-3889R. At 15 shares, 1R
$45, gross loss $150, costs still $5, net -$155/-3.4444R. Gross R stays -3-3333; net R worsens
slightly because the flat fee is a larger share of planned risk.
Pause & try it
Recalculate GAPS at 15 rather than 30 shares, including the $5 flat round-trip cost. Give price-
risk 1R, notional, gross/net loss, net R, cash after entry and final cash. Explain what changes and
what remains constant.
case-studies-answers-33.png:
15 shares at $80 with stop $77: price-risk 1R = $45, notional $1,200. Entry debit $1,202.50 leaves
$18,797.50. Exit at $70 credits $1,047.50, giving $19,845 final cash. Gross -$150; costs $5; net -
$155.
Gross R = -150/45 = -3-3333; net R = -155/45 = -3.4444. Dollar loss falls but the gross multiple
remains unchanged. A fixed fee causes the net multiple to worsen; redefining R after the gap would
hide this.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Audit the ambiguous account
Use P1's conventions on an unfamiliar fictional bar: a $20,000 account, 40 shares filled at
$25.00, stop $24.00, target $27.00, $5 round-trip cost and stop-first resolution of an ambiguous
bar. (a) The first held bar is 025.20/H27.30/L23.80/C26.10. Give 1R, the stop-first and target-first
net results in dollars and R, the ending cash under each, and the size of the difference. (b)
Suppose instead the bar is 023.90/H27.30/L23.80/C26.10. What does P1 record, and why is there
no sequence ambiguity? (c) Write the review sentence that keeps the modeled result separate
from what the bar can show.
(a) 1R = 40 × ($25.00 - $24.00) = $40. The open $25.20 lies between the levels, and the bar reaches
both. Stop-first: 40 × (24.00 - 25.00) = -$40 gross, -$45 net, -45 ÷ 40 = -1.125R; ending cash
$20,000 - $45 = $19,955. Target-first: 40 × (27.00 - 25.00) = +$80 gross, +$75 net, +1.875R;
ending cash $20,075. The difference is $120, or exactly 3R, and it comes entirely from the assumed
order of trades inside one bar.
case-studies-answers-34.png:
(b) The open $23.90 is already below the $24.00 stop, so P1's opening-gap priority exits at the open
before any later high is considered: 40 × (23.90 - 25.00) = -$44 gross, -$49 net, - 49 ÷ 40 =
-1.225R. The 1R denominator stays $40. The later $27-30 high cannot have been reached by a
position that had already exited.
(c) For (a): "Modeled stop-first result -$45/-1.125R under P1's declared convention; the bar touched
both levels and the true sequence is unresolved from daily OHLC." Full credit requires the fill-model
label, the original $40 denominator, the $5 cost in both branches and no claim about the actual
intraday order.

Transfer to sparse historical facts
The historical GME extract supplies closes and an intraday high but no full OHLC window or
opening quote. Which pieces of P1 can be evaluated, and which facts would you request before
modeling an order?
Price changes between supplied closes can be calculated. The extract cannot establish Pi's previously

regular-session OHLC and quotes/timing. Do not substitute the later high for an executable exit.

First read the information cutoff and cover the continuation. State what is observed, what is

frozen rule, including a skip or an unresolved state when appropriate. Third reconcile the result
and ask which conclusion it supports. This procedure turns a case from a memorable story into
something another reader can reproduce.
The first seven cases below are fictional, purpose-built to exercise different decisions. The

announcement, and a calendar-selected AAPL/MSFT/SPY gallery with exact archived OHLC.
The gallery preserves its complete selection ledger and a separately disclosed ambiguity

Use the completed P1 plan from Chapter 21 for the shared breakout cases. For ATLS, BRDG,

beginning
At So the only price-based signal fact is C50.40 > previously frozen 50.00. In both branches
the opening offer is $50.60 and a supplied paper execution confirms 50 shares at that price
during Pi's allowed hour. The entry debit is $2,532.50 including its $2.50 charge; 1R freezes at

Case three: the skip is a completed decision

execution fact. Each filled result reports its own frozen price-risk denominator and its separate

application; they were not sampled from a real opportunity set. A count of winners in the
gallery would mostly measure the author's selection. Chapter 24 shows how a frozen research
rule and chronological evaluation window address a different question.

when an execution claim must stop; the calendar-selected archive gallery supplies small OHLC
windows with retrospective adjustments and undocumented session details. Apply the same
three-pass method: freeze the stated clock, identify missing inputs and distinguish later

Historical case selection and data conventions
The historical cases below were selected to teach two data problems: an event-driven price
move and a share-unit change. Selection is purposive, based on publicly documented episodes,
rather than a random screen or an outcome-blind trading sample. Both the surge and
subsequent fall in the selected GME episode are included. These cases cannot estimate a hit
rate. Use the fictional cases earlier in the chapter to rehearse fully specified execution; these
historical records teach what can and cannot be inferred from limited observations.
Provenance: GME, January 12-28, 2021, is reconstructed from SEC statf report section 3.2,
printed pp. 18-19, published October 14, 2021. Prices use the dollar/share units reported for
that period, not a later split-adjusted chart. Reported closing prices are distinguished from
intraday highs; the report does not supply a complete OHLC series or exact timestamps for the
highs. No dividend reinvestment or price adjustment is performed here. Two closes are derived
from explicitly reported daily dollar changes, with the arithmetic disclosed in the table. Missing
sessions remain missing.
Reuse basis: the SEC's Webmaster FAQ states that Government-created site content is free to
access and reuse, while some content such as stock art is excluded. This book attributes a few
numeric facts from the staff report and makes its own table and diagram; it copies no vendor
chart, artwork or logo. The FAQ is not a license for a vendor's underlying market-data feed. The
Apple case paraphrases the issuer's dated announcement and uses original algebra, with no
copied chart or photo.
GME event reaction: a large move still leaves execution
unknown
At the January 13 close, compare the two completed closing observations and volumes shown
in the first panel. Price change is 31.40 - 19.95 = $11.45, or 57.39%; approximate share volume
is roughly 20 times the previous session (about 144 million against 7 million shares). These are
observations. The words "breakout" or "short squeeze" add an interpretation whose definition
and evidence must be supplied.

Apple's 2014 split: change the unit before classifying a
break
Apple announced a seven-for-one stock split on April 23, 2014, with a June 2 record date and
split-adjusted trading beginning June 9. This corporate-action case is selected to test unit
consistency, independently of any later return. The announcement is usable as an event-
calendar fact after its release; it supplies no entry or target prices.
At a June 6 analysis cutoff, the announced unit change belongs in the data plan for the next
session. If a pre-split price is P and volume is V, a consistently split-adjusted comparison
expresses that prior price as P/7 and prior share volume as 7V. A holder of N shares becomes a
holder of 7N shares, so NP = (7N)(P/7) before other price movement. P, V and N are algebraic
placeholders, not historical quotes. No dollar P&L is inferred. A raw discontinuity caused by
the share unit is not evidence of a structural support failure.
Decision record: request a daily feed with its adjustment convention and the corporate-action
flag before drawing a June 9 candle or computing a moving average across the date. The
supplied announcement alone leads to a data-check decision, not a trade. This makes "skip" a
completed analysis with a reason, rather than an empty chart opinion.
A calendar-selected historical gallery: freeze the
procedure first
The next gallery gives you a complete small OHLC window rather than a handful of famous-
event facts. Before downloading prices, we fixed three symbols-Apple (AAPL), Microsoft
(MSFT) and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) - and every month of 2016. The cutoff is the first
available archive session on or after each month's first day. Every one of the 36 symbol-month
cells stays in the ledger. The symbols and year are teaching choices, not a historical investable
universe; choosing familiar surviving securities introduces a selection limit even when dates
are chosen without looking at their outcomes.
The exercise gate is deliberately simple: compare the cutoff close C with the arithmetic mean of
the five preceding closes, excluding C. If C'is not strictly higher, record "skipped." If it is higher,
observe the next five archive sessions against an upper level of 1.01C and a lower level of 0.99C.
A session opening at or beyond a level resolves that side first. Otherwise compare its high and
low: a sole upper touch is "favorable," a sole lower touch "adverse," and touching both in that
first resolving bar is "ambiguous." No touch within five sessions is "ordinary/unresolved."
These labels describe a price path under an invented exercise rule. They are not successful or
failed historical trades.
case-studies-learner-17.png:
The full ledger below contains 18 skips, six favorable paths, eleven adverse paths and one
ordinary/unresolved path; none is an ambiguous first resolving bar. We show the earliest
example of each represented class, with alphabetical symbol order breaking date ties. This
representative choice is intentionally outcome-stratified, so the four illustrations are not a
sample from which to estimate probabilities. Do not divide favorable counts by eligible counts
to infer a strategy's success rate. There is no order, position, fill, stop execution, cash account,
commission model or held-out strategy test.
Provenance and reuse: Boris Marjanovic's Huge Stock Market Dataset on Kaggle, version 3,
provides the three daily files. Retrieved metadata explicitly declares CCo-1.0, and the depositor
states that prices are adjusted for dividends and splits. We copied numeric observations into
original tables and diagrams. The stated permission is the depositor's; metadata does not
identify an upstream provider or establish others' rights. The local source snapshots, exact
download URLs, SHA-256 hashes, extracts and frozen selection sheet are preserved in
data/historical/ for independent inspection.
Data conventions: source date labels and all OHLC decimals are retained, in the archive's
adjusted dollar scale. Daily aggregation is reported, but exact regular/extended-session
inclusion, time zone and adjustment formula are undocumented, and the adjustment vintage is
bounded only by the depositor's note "last updated 11/10/2017". We therefore call them archive
sessions, not certified regular-session candles. No missing date is interpolated. Volume is
unused because its adjustment convention is unspecified. These are retrospectively adjusted
records, not a reconstruction of prices published at each 2016 cutoff. The cutoff exercise hides
future bars; it does not make the adjusted vintage contemporaneous. Before modeling real
transactions, obtain documented raw quotes, corporate actions, precise sessions, spread and
order information.

THE IDEA TO KEEP

One line, one deliberate loss of detail
Imagine following a stock whose daily closes alternate between small advances and retreats.
The individual marks can make its direction hard to describe. A moving average replaces each
eligible observation with a summary of recent observations. You gain a simpler view, but you
surrender information about their order and their extremes. Two quite different paths can have
the same average. Begin by asking which detail you are willing to remove and why.
moving-averages-answers-2.png:
Fidelity defines a simple moving average, or SMA, as an arithmetic average over a specified
period. Here the input is the closing price: SMA at time t equals the sum of the latest N closes
divided by N. Five daily closes describe five sessions; five weekly closes describe five weeks. The
parameter names a number of observations, rather than a universal duration.
Calculate it, then watch what leaves
For fictional closes of $10, $11, $12, $13, and $14, the five-session SMA is $12. If the next close
is $15, the $10 observation leaves and $15 enters, producing $13. Notice that an average can
move substantially because an old outlier leaves, even when today's change is small. An
indicator has a memory structure; understanding that structure prevents you from attributing
every movement in its line to something new in the market.
This textbook leaves the SMA undefined until all N observations exist. An implementation that
averages only the observations available at the beginning produces a different early series.
Adjusted versus unadjusted prices also change the input. Before comparing two charting
systems, match the price field, session, adjustment policy, and missing-data handling. A
smooth line is only as coherent as the data underneath it.

Exponential weighting and the first value
An exponential moving average, or EMA, updates a prior average rather than dropping the
oldest observation completely. A common convention is EMA today = alpha x close today + (1
- alpha) × EMA yesterday, with alpha = 2/(N + 1). For N = 5, alpha is one third. Fidelity
describes using an SMA for the first EMA value. In our five-session example, seed the EMA at
$12; the next $15 close produces $13.
On the following $15 close, the five-session SMA becomes $13.80, while the EMA becomes
approximately $13.67. An EMA responds more to the newest price than the same-length SMA,
but individual comparisons need not follow a simple ranking because the rest of the history
matters. A seed's influence decays by repeated multiplication by 1 - alpha. Record the seed and
warm-up history, especially in short samples.
The price of smoothing is delay
A longer lookback generally suppresses more local variation. It also carries older observations
farther into the description of today. If a stock changes direction abruptly, those observations
keep pulling the average toward the former regime. That is the source of lag. No choice
eliminates both noise and delay. A very responsive setting exposes you to small fluctuations; a
slower setting can remain persuasive after the underlying behavior has changed.
Suppose fictional price jumps from a long sequence near $20 to $24. An average below $24 is
not an independent discovery that the stock is cheap. It is the arithmetic consequence of
retaining earlier prices. Likewise, touching an average does not force a bounce. Use phrases
such as "price returned to its recent mean" before adding a hypothesis about what participants
might do there.
Observe the first state, then count crossings
At session 5 of the main table, close $14 exceeds the newly available SMA $12. This is the first
classified state, not a crossover: session 4 has no eligible mean. At session 7, $15 remains above
$13.80. At session 8, $14 falls below $14.20 after the preceding close was above its own
average. This first downward crossing is observable after session 8 closes.
Freeze this teaching definition: up means today's close exceeds its eligible SMA after yesterday
was at or below its eligible SMA; down means today is at or below after yesterday was above.
Both averages must exist. Equality belongs to the below-or-equal side. The definition identifies
an analysis event, without assuming an execution at its closing price.

One line, one deliberate loss of detail
Imagine following a stock whose daily closes alternate between small advances and retreats.
The individual marks can make its direction hard to describe. A moving average replaces each
eligible observation with a summary of recent observations. You gain a simpler view, but you
surrender information about their order and their extremes. Two quite different paths can have
the same average. Begin by asking which detail you are willing to remove and why.
moving-averages-learner-2.png:
Fidelity defines a simple moving average, or SMA, as an arithmetic average over a specified
period. Here the input is the closing price: SMA at time t equals the sum of the latest N closes
divided by N. Five daily closes describe five sessions; five weekly closes describe five weeks. The
parameter names a number of observations, rather than a universal duration.
Calculate it, then watch what leaves
For fictional closes of $10, $11, $12, $13, and $14, the five-session SMA is $12. If the next close
is $15, the $10 observation leaves and $15 enters, producing $13. Notice that an average can
move substantially because an old outlier leaves, even when today's change is small. An
indicator has a memory structure; understanding that structure prevents you from attributing
every movement in its line to something new in the market.
This textbook leaves the SMA undefined until all N observations exist. An implementation that
averages only the observations available at the beginning produces a different early series.
Adjusted versus unadjusted prices also change the input. Before comparing two charting
systems, match the price field, session, adjustment policy, and missing-data handling. A
smooth line is only as coherent as the data underneath it.

Evidence review: evaluate a claim, then
process a system

Solution edition: includes every worked solution.
Convert a performance claim into checkable
arithmetic
A fictional locked study has 10 nonoverlapping trades, each 1R $8o: four gross +2R, five -1R, one
-2R gap. Flat costs $4/trade. Account starts $10,000 with fixed-dollar sizing. Compute gross/net
expectancy, net account return and flat break-even cost. Can it validate the rule?
Gross R = 8-5-2 = 1R; gross $8o. Costs $40 = 0.5R, net $40 = 0.5R; gross expectancy 0.10R and net
0.05R. Net account return $40 ÷ $10,000 = 0.4% (gross 0.8%); break-even $80 ÷ 10 = $8 per round
trip. It cannot validate the rule, and not merely because the data are invented. Net R per trade is
+1.95 (x4), -1.05 (x5) and -2.05; the sample SD is about 1.66R and the standard error about 0.53R,
so the rough +2 SE band (about -1.00R to +1.10R) includes zero. Dropping one winner makes the
mean -0.16R, and the $8 break-even is only twice the assumed $4 cost. Ten trades with no
comparator or independent window cannot validate a rule.
Allocate simultaneous candidates
A simplified Atlas-20 variant has equity E = $50,000, of which $12,000 is cash; its four held
positions have risen since entry, and they occupy four of the five slots. Use a $2 stop distance, a 0.5%
price-risk allowance, a 10% notional cap measured at the limit price, and a cash allowance of (cash -

$2.50 entry fee) ÷ limit; round each allowance down to whole shares, and reserve shares × limit +
$2.50. Eligible A: close 40.00, prior-20 high 39.00. Eligible B: close 20.40, prior-20 high 20.00.
Rank by breakout margin, 100 x (close - prior-20 high) ÷ prior-2o high, rounded to o.o1 percentage
point. Each limit is close × 1.01, rounded down to the cent. Which candidate gets the order, how
many shares, and what cash reserve?
A's margin = 100 x (40.00 - 39.00) ÷ 39.00 = 2.5641..., which rounds to 2.56%; B's = 100 × 0.40 ÷
20.00 = 2.00%, so A ranks first. A's limit = 40.00 x 1.01 = $40.40. Allowances: risk floor(0.5% x
$50,000 ÷ $2) = floor(250 ÷ 2) = 125 shares; notional floor($5,000 ÷ $40.40) = 123; cash
floor($11,997.50 ÷ $40.40) = 296. The smallest, 123, is the order, so the notional cap binds; planned
1R = 123 × $2 = $246, inside the $250 budget. Reserve 123 × $40.40 + $2.50 = $4,971.70, leaving
$7,028.30 available. B stays eligible but gets no slot and is not re-offered later. Filled risk is fixed by
the actual fill; there is no later substitution without a new decision.
Identify the research clock
A researcher logs six variants on 2015-19 data and locks one by a pre-written rule. Run once on held-
out 2020-21 data, it averages +0.02R over 14 trades. After charting the held-out losers, she adds a
filter: trade only if, within the prior 20 sessions, a completed low fell at least 1% below range support
frozen before that low, and a close strictly above support followed within the breach session or the
next three sessions, no later than the breakout's decision close. On 2020-21 the filtered version earns
+0.31R over 8 trades. (a) Label both results. (b) How many variants has the search now tried, and
under Chapter 25's independence model what is the chance that at least one no-edge variant passes a
5% test? (c) At which close is each filter event first known? (d) What data may evaluate the new
version, and what must be frozen first?
(a) The locked result, +0.02R over 14 trades, stays the held-out result for v1 as recorded. The filtered
+0.31R is development evidence for a new version, v2: its 8 trades are a subset of the 14, kept after
their outcomes were seen, and the 2020-21 window shaped the filter, so it is not a held-out test.
(b) Seven variants. If each were an independent 5% test of a rule with no edge, 1 - 0.957 = 0.302,
about 30%; variants that share trades make the true figure different, but reporting only the survivor
still overstates the evidence. (c) Each filter event is known only at the close that returns above
support, not at the breach low; using it earlier is look-ahead. (d) Only a fresh window or a paper

The problem is judgment under uncertainty
Technical analysis involves looking for structure in noisy observations. That makes it easy to
mistake an explanation that feels coherent for an explanation that has earned confidence. You
can describe a chart eloquently while leaving its predictive claim untested. Good psychological
practice begins by accepting that an uncertain decision can produce either outcome.
Maya's BRDG-P1 trade connects this chapter with the completed plan. The initial
interpretation was continuation beyond $50; the supplied path is revealed after the cutoff
attempt. The same note could instead precede a rally. The exercise is to preserve what she
knew, then grade what she did, with the outcome recorded in its own field. The figures and
counterfactuals are fictional, constructed to make the comparison inspectable.
A price is not a personal obligation
The disposition effect describes a tendency to realize gains more readily than losses. The SEC-
hosted Library of Congress investor-behavior review discusses this among several potentially
harmful investing behaviors. This is a description of observed tendencies, not a diagnosis of
every trader or proof about the motive behind a particular trade.
Maya buys at $40 and plans an exit if her specific hypothesis fails near $38. Price reaches
$37.80. She changes the rationale to "I will wait until it gets back to $40." Her purchase price
has become a psychological reference point even though it does not oblige future buyers to
transact there. The key process failure is the unrecorded change in hypothesis. A fresh long-
term investment thesis could be evaluated separately, but silently converting a short trade into
that thesis prevents a fair assessment of either decision.
Confirmation becomes an editing habit
Suppose Maya believes a breakout is forming. She notices a rising moving average and ignores
weak sector performance. Then she searches only for commentary supporting the rally. Each
supporting observation may be real; the problem is that the selection rule favors her initial
conclusion. Adding more agreeable indicators can create an appearance of corroboration
without adding independent information.
psychology-answers-05.png:
Try a concrete counterargument exercise. Before committing, write the strongest observable
reason the trade might fail. For BRDG this could be a prior breakout that quickly reentered the
range, an upcoming event, or an entry price already far from the planned invalidation. Next
specify what new observation would change the decision. This exercise is a proposed discipline,
not a proven treatment with a guaranteed return benefit. Its usefulness comes from exposing
the criteria you are actually using.
Outcome bias and hindsight work together
A rule violation followed by profit can look brilliant in the journal. A careful decision followed
by loss can look foolish. This is outcome-based grading. It becomes more misleading when
hindsight changes the remembered difficulty of the original decision. After a rally, yesterday's
ambiguity can feel like an obvious opportunity; after a decline, the same setup can feel
obviously defective.
Freeze a short note and screenshot at the decision time, showing only information then
available. Record an estimated scenario range rather than a single confident target. After the
outcome, compare that frozen view with the narrative you now feel tempted to tell. If your
original note considered both breakout and failure, keep both visible. Do not rewrite
uncertainty as certainty merely because the next ten bars resolved it. A loss can teach
something without proving that the initial choice was irrational.
Read one frozen note against its continuation
The table is Maya's actual completed note in the fictional paper exercise, recorded after So and
before S1. It does not claim three independent reasons to buy. The completed close crosses the
boundary; the upper shadow supplies a concrete counterobservation. These are both derived
from the same candle, so counting them as statistically independent evidence would be a
mistake. The record also says which context data were not supplied, rather than filling that
field with an agreeable story.
Hide the continuation and ask what this note licenses. It licenses applying P1 at the next
opening opportunity. It does not license buying at the already completed So close, increasing
quantity after a losing week, or widening the stop because the word "retest" sounds reassuring.
It explicitly allows the continuation hypothesis to weaken before the operational stop executes.
Keeping those two conditions distinct makes it possible to evaluate both the interpretation and
the exit rule.
Now reveal the appended record. At S2, the $49.60 close is back below the range edge; at S3,
the supplied stop model produces - $105 net. Maya may feel she should have "known" the

Make pressure smaller and decisions slower
Imagine that Maya doubles her normal position after three losses because she wants to recover
the week immediately. The next trade may still meet her chart criteria, but its size now
responds to a financial and emotional deadline rather than the documented risk policy. It is
useful to separate the signal decision from the exposure decision: a qualifying signal does not
authorize any share count she happens to want.
Possible constraints include a maximum aggregate exposure, a waiting period before
discretionary rule changes, and a pause in new entries when she cannot explain the plan
calmly. These are examples to evaluate, not universal psychological prescriptions. A smaller
paper exercise may reveal whether the process is understandable without the urgency of
money. If repeatedly monitoring positions disrupts sleep or necessary work, that information
belongs in the decision about whether this activity fits her life.
Calibration is more useful than bravado
A forecast is calibrated when events assigned similar probabilities occur at comparable
frequencies over many relevant observations. If Maya labels ten scenarios "70% likely" and six
occur, one small group is insufficient to declare her well or poorly calibrated. She needs a larger
record, consistent event definitions, and awareness that market conditions can change. Even a
well-calibrated forecast may offer no worthwhile trade after costs.

Reconcile the unfamiliar cutoff note
One defensible Qo note is: "The completed $64.40 close is above the frozen $64 boundary; its
$0.30 upper shadow is a counterobservation from the same candle, not independent sector
evidence. Apply L1 only if the opening quote and fill conditions pass. A completed close below
$64 would weaken continuation without rewriting the standing exits." Another supplied
observation may receive different weight; the rubric rewards a timestamp and bounded
inference.
The fictional reveal supplies a Q1 09:30 ET opening ask of $64.60, above $62.60 and no higher
than $64.90. A confirmed paper execution report then fills all 50 shares at $64.60 at 09:31,
within the $64.90 limit and first-hour window; no remainder is left. The Q2 close is $63.60
and the supplied position report confirms that no standing exit has executed. At Q3, the
supplied stop execution report closes the 50 shares at $62.60, with no earlier target or gap exit.
These reports are scenario inputs, not facts inferred from daily closes. Filled price-risk is 50 x
(64.60 - 62.60) = $100; gross result -$100, fees $5 and net -$105/-1.05R. Cash falls by
$3,232.50 at entry and receives $3,127.50 at exit, ending at $19,895. The weakening
observation appeared before the modeled exit. Keep the original note unchanged, record a
compliant loss separately from the failed continuation hypothesis, and propose any new close-
exit rule only for future evaluation.

The BRDG-P1 note earlier in this reference is a shared worked rehearsal whose outcome
readers may already know from Chapter 21. Reconstructing it cannot demonstrate a fresh
prospective decision. The unfamiliar Qo packet is the chapter's attempt-first exercise; neither a

Observation does not prove an intervention
Barber and Odean's brokerage sample connects turnover with net performance after trading
costs. It does not assign people to journal, pause or counterargument exercises. The process
proposals in this chapter aim to make decisions inspectable; this edition supplies no
experiment showing that they improve returns.
A WORKED EXAMPLE
The lucky violation
The same fictional winning path earns +2 times initial price risk before costs. At the
documented $100 risk size it would earn $200. Maya instead quadruples quantity and risks
$400 without a recorded reason, earning $800 on that same path. Assume proportional fills
and omit costs for this comparison. The gain is real in the scenario; it supplies no evidence that
breaking the documented sizing policy was a sound decision. Grade policy adherence and
outcome in separate fields.
Pause & try it
For rehearsal, reconstruct a four-field S0 note from 049.90/H50.70/L49.70/C50.40 and the $50
boundary, then reconcile the already explained P1 continuation (S2 C49.60 and the S3 modeled
stop). Keep observation, counterargument, conditional action and weakening condition separate.
Because the shared P1 outcome has appeared in Chapter 21 and this chapter, this reconstruction
is not a prospective learning test; attempt the unfamiliar LARK cutoff packet first.
One defensible note: "C50.40 is above the prior $50 edge. The close is $0.30 below its high; this one
candle does not show independent sector support. Apply P1 only if the next opening gate and account
checks pass. A completed close below $50 weakens continuation; P1 still exits via its declared
stop/target/time rules." Other observable counterarguments are acceptable if supplied before the
outcome.
psychology-answers-12.png:
Afterward: S2 close 49.60 meets the named weakening observation; S3 modeled stop yields -
$105/-1.05R. Grade P1 compliance separately from loss. Keep the So note unchanged. Full credit
requires no use of S1-S3 data in the initial note and no invented probability.
GUIDED PRACTICE
Hold the winning path constant
The documented position carries $100 price risk and its winning path earns +2R gross. A
violation quadruples the shares. Calculate both gross results and both net results under a fixed
$5 modeled round-trip fee.
Documented: $200 gross/$195 net. Quadrupled: $800 gross/$795 net. Own frozen R denominators
are $100 and $400, so net R is +1.95 and +1.9875. Different fee fractions explain the difference;
neither establishes that the violation was justified.
INDEPENDENT PRACTICE
Write a useful revision hypothesis
After the loss, Maya writes "I should always exit a failed breakout early!" Turn this into a
prospective rule proposal and explain which data remain development data.
One proposal: P2 exits at the next feasible opening price after any completed close below the original
boundary, unless the standing stop/target has already exited. Declare whether a close-exit request
replaces or supplements standing orders. Compare P2 with P1 on later opportunities, including
rebounds after reentry.
The BRDG loss motivated the proposal and remains development evidence. It is not a fresh test of P2.
The rubric rewards a timestamp, price field, order priority and prospective comparator; no particular
threshold is required.

One question before you go
After S2 closes below $50, Maya labels the original P1 trade "noncompliant" because it did not exit at

outcome, compare that frozen view with the narrative you now feel tempted to tell. If your
original note considered both breakout and failure, keep both visible. Do not rewrite
uncertainty as certainty merely because the next ten bars resolved it. A loss can teach
something without proving that the initial choice was irrational.
Read one frozen note against its continuation
The table is Maya's actual completed note in the fictional paper exercise, recorded after So and
before S1. It does not claim three independent reasons to buy. The completed close crosses the
boundary; the upper shadow supplies a concrete counterobservation. These are both derived
from the same candle, so counting them as statistically independent evidence would be a
mistake. The record also says which context data were not supplied, rather than filling that
field with an agreeable story.
Hide the continuation and ask what this note licenses. It licenses applying P1 at the next
opening opportunity. It does not license buying at the already completed So close, increasing
quantity after a losing week, or widening the stop because the word "retest" sounds reassuring.
It explicitly allows the continuation hypothesis to weaken before the operational stop executes.
Keeping those two conditions distinct makes it possible to evaluate both the interpretation and
the exit rule.
Now reveal the appended record. At S2, the $49.60 close is back below the range edge; at S3,
the supplied stop model produces - $105 net. Maya may feel she should have "known" the

breakout would fail. Compare that impression with the unchanged So note. It recognized both
possibilities and supplied no probability. The correct update is that this continuation failed. A
statement that the original outcome was obvious would add certainty that the original record
did not contain.
There is a reasonable alternative editorial reading: the So upper shadow is not compelling
counterevidence and may deserve little weight. Another analyst might focus on a prior failure
or sector weakness if those data were supplied. The rubric asks for an observable
counterargument and a clear limit on the inference, not agreement with Maya's chosen
weighting. Both readers must distinguish a new interpretation from changing Pi's written
orders.
The same process can record a winning violation. Suppose Maya bought 200 rather than 50
shares at $50.60 without revising the risk authorization, and this time the path reached
$54.60. Price gain would be $800 instead of $200; under the plan's flat $5 cost assumption the
net figures would be $795 and $195. That modeled fee convention is kept constant for this
counterfactual, while actual liquidity might make such proportional fills unrealistic. Profit
scales with quantity on the same path; policy adherence does not become better because the
sign is positive.

Make pressure smaller and decisions slower
Imagine that Maya doubles her normal position after three losses because she wants to recover
the week immediately. The next trade may still meet her chart criteria, but its size now
responds to a financial and emotional deadline rather than the documented risk policy. It is
useful to separate the signal decision from the exposure decision: a qualifying signal does not
authorize any share count she happens to want.
Possible constraints include a maximum aggregate exposure, a waiting period before
discretionary rule changes, and a pause in new entries when she cannot explain the plan
calmly. These are examples to evaluate, not universal psychological prescriptions. A smaller
paper exercise may reveal whether the process is understandable without the urgency of
money. If repeatedly monitoring positions disrupts sleep or necessary work, that information
belongs in the decision about whether this activity fits her life.
Calibration is more useful than bravado
A forecast is calibrated when events assigned similar probabilities occur at comparable
frequencies over many relevant observations. If Maya labels ten scenarios "70% likely" and six
occur, one small group is insufficient to declare her well or poorly calibrated. She needs a larger
record, consistent event definitions, and awareness that market conditions can change. Even a
well-calibrated forecast may offer no worthwhile trade after costs.

Observation does not prove an intervention
Barber and Odean's brokerage sample connects turnover with net performance after trading
costs. It does not assign people to journal, pause or counterargument exercises. The process
proposals in this chapter aim to make decisions inspectable; this edition supplies no
experiment showing that they improve returns.

and omit costs for this comparison. The gain is real in the scenario; it supplies no evidence that
breaking the documented sizing policy was a sound decision. Grade policy adherence and
outcome in separate fields.

A small number of areas beats an all-purpose drawing
The construction above gives a reason for including one zone and excluding several nearby
marks. A resistance exercise uses interrupted advances instead: select declared local peaks,
cluster their prices under a stated span tolerance, and freeze the resulting area before testing
the next visit. The independent practice gives you a fresh example. This symmetry helps you
build a map rather than memorize one picture.
If every price gets a line, almost every turn can be explained afterward as near something. A
useful map is sparse enough to be challenged. Count a visit only under the declared field and
cutoff, then describe whether the reaction definition occurred. The more careful wording is
"these prior closing troughs form this area" and "the later data met or did not meet this
condition." Supply-and-demand explanations can remain hypotheses while the measurements
are precise.
A plausible mechanism has a market boundary
Osler's order data provide a concrete example of round-number clustering in currency markets.
They do not reveal the orders near Harbor's fictional zone or test a stock support rule. Keep the
mechanism as a hypothesis until the relevant stock data and executable rule have been
evaluated.

A small number of areas beats an all-purpose drawing
The construction above gives a reason for including one zone and excluding several nearby
marks. A resistance exercise uses interrupted advances instead: select declared local peaks,
cluster their prices under a stated span tolerance, and freeze the resulting area before testing
the next visit. The independent practice gives you a fresh example. This symmetry helps you
build a map rather than memorize one picture.
If every price gets a line, almost every turn can be explained afterward as near something. A
useful map is sparse enough to be challenged. Count a visit only under the declared field and
cutoff, then describe whether the reaction definition occurred. The more careful wording is
"these prior closing troughs form this area" and "the later data met or did not meet this
condition." Supply-and-demand explanations can remain hypotheses while the measurements
are precise.

system-design-answers-02.png:
Start with an economic question
A trading system is an organized set of decisions that can be applied consistently. It need not be
automated, but its rules should be clear enough to evaluate. Begin with a proposed mechanism
and an observable claim. "Trends may persist over this horizon" is a research hypothesis. "This
indicator predicts everything" is not a useful specification. The mechanism does not prove an
edge; it tells you what evidence would support or weaken the idea.
Chapter 24 tested a twenty-session breakout signal one trade at a time, as though capital and
position slots were unlimited. This chapter builds Atlas-20, a complete fictional research
system around the same kind of daily breakout signal, and makes every remaining decision
explicit. It freezes version 1.o of the rule sheet, supplies a small invented market of eight stocks
over eight sessions, and processes each decision in order until the ledger reconciles to the cent.
All companies, prices, volumes, and calendars are fictional. The percentages are teaching
settings, not recommended allocations, and the system has no demonstrated performance. The
scenario was built to exercise the rules, including a tie, a partial fill, an unfilled order, a halt,
and other exceptions, so it is not a typical week.
Use one test for completeness: two careful readers given the same inputs should produce the
same ledger without asking the author anything. Each rule below is labeled as a definition, a
modeling convention, a scope choice, or an arbitrary teaching setting. The included
scripts/atlas20-sim.cjs processes the supplied scenario under the rule sheet and reproduces its
accounting; it is a teaching simulator, not a trading engine. You can also reproduce every
number by hand from this chapter's tables.
Write the data and eligibility contract
Atlas-20 uses a point-in-time universe and completed regular-session daily bars. "Point in
time" means the system uses the member list, prices, and calendar as they were known at each
decision close, not as they are known today. The signal needs the twenty sessions before the
decision day, so a stock needs 21 consecutive valid bars before it can be screened. If any of
those bars is missing, v1.o records an incomplete record and evaluates nothing that day. It does
not fill the gap with yesterday's price, because an invented bar could create or hide a breakout.
Each filter is part of the research claim, so each is stated with its data and timing. The liquidity
filter averages close x volume over the twenty sessions ending at the decision close. A cutoff
chosen from the full sample would quietly use the future. The price band keeps the fixed $2
stop between 2% and 10% of the share price. Without it, the same rule would mean very
different risks for a $15 stock and a $150 stock. The earnings exclusion covers sessions t+1
through t+10 because this is the planned ten-session holding window for an entry in t+1
system-design-answers-03.png:
(holding session 1), ending at t+10 (holding session 10), so entries exclude announcements
known at the decision close within that window. A rescheduled or unexpected announcement
remains possible; the calendar is not insurance. The checks run in a declared order, and the
first failure is recorded. That keeps the record of skipped candidates honest. A halt can extend
the actual elapsed holding beyond that planned window; the calendar filter cannot exclude
every announcement during an overdue holding.

An eligible stock signals when its completed close exceeds the highest high of the prior twenty

percentage point, as stated in the table; ties in that rounded value are broken alphabetically.

At most five slots exist, and a slot is occupied by any open position, including a halted one, and

The cash test deserves a remark. Five slots at a 10% notional cap can commit only about half of
equity, so cash does not bind in this unleveraged, mildly varying scenario. Large mark changes,
stale valuations, or a later version can make the cash test important; the entry caps do not
bound subsequent market values. It is still computed at every decision, for two reasons.
Reservations must prevent the same dollars from funding two orders, and any later version
with larger caps or more slots can make cash bind. One of the practice tasks shows such a

Exits, gaps, and time are first-class rules
Entries use a day-limit buy order for the next session at 1.01 x the signal close, rounded down
to the cent. Investor.gov explains that a buy limit executes only at its limit or lower and is not
guaranteed to execute, and that a day order generally cancels at the end of the regular session.
Atlas-20 models those facts with deliberately conservative conventions. An open at or below
the limit fills at the open. A later trade strictly below the limit fills at the limit. A low exactly
equal to the limit shows only that the price was touched, which does not prove that shares were
available, so it is not a fill. The filled quantity is capped at 1% of the session's share volume, and
the rest of the order is canceled.
system-design-answers-06.png:
Each fill receives a sell stop $2.00 below and a sell limit target $4.00 above the actual fill price,
plus a time exit at the close of the tenth holding session. Investor.gov notes that a stop becomes
a market order once its price is reached and can execute well away from that price. Atlas-20
therefore models an ordinary stop at the stop price, an opening gap through the stop at the
open, and a bar that contains both levels as a stop. Daily data cannot show which level traded
first, and assuming the favorable order would flatter the record. These are assumptions about
fills, not reports of actual executions.
A trading halt is a different problem. According to Investor.gov, the most common regulatory
halt occurs when news is pending, and securities exchanges, not the SEC, decide whether to
impose it; other U.S. markets honor a halt imposed by the security's primary market. While a
held stock has no bar, no exit can be modeled. Atlas-20 marks the stock at its last valid close,
flags that mark as stale, keeps the slot occupied, and applies the gap rule to the first new bar.
Cash earns nothing, settlement timing is ignored, and short sales, leverage, and derivatives are
outside the scope of v1.0.
The 1% volume cap is a retrospective daily-bar fill model: the total session volume is unknown

revisions during these eight sessions; a deployment specification would need separate policies

for this exercise, not a full historical feed.

Session 1 begins with the held positions. Hazel's range stays between its $45 stop and $51
target. Fir's low of $34.60 stays above its $34.00 stop. Next come the entries. Alder opens at
$32.10, below its $32.27 limit, so all 250 shares fill at the open. Its stop is $30.10, its target is
$36.10, and IR is $500. Birch opens at $72.20, within its limit, but only 11,800 shares trade, so
the 1% cap allows 118 of the 138 shares ordered. The remainder cancels, and Birch's 1R is 118 x
$2 = $236, not the $276 planned at the order. Cedar opens at $41.60, above its $41.20 limit,
and its low is exactly $41.20. That is a touch, so there is no fill, and the $9,972.90 reservation is
released. Cash falls from $81,330.00 by $8,027.50 and $8,522.10 to $64,780.40, and equity at
the close is $100,028.30.
Cedar's unused slot does not go back to Dogwood, because candidates are offered only at their
own signal close. Dogwood earns a new chance by signaling again at decision close 1: its $62.40
close exceeds the new prior-20 high of $61.50. The 158-share order reflects the notional
allowance, floor(10,002.83 ÷ 63.02). In session 2, Dogwood opens at $62.80, below its limit,
and fills there. Hazel reaches holding session 10 without touching either level and exits at the
$49.30 close for +$455 net, or +1.14R on its $400 denominator. At decision close 2, Cedar
signals again at $42.30, above the $41.95 high it set in session 1, and receives a 234-share order
at $42.72.
In session 3, Fir has no bar: trading is halted. Fir is marked at its session-2 close of $35.10 and
flagged stale, and the missing bar fires an operational review trigger. Cedar opens at $43.00,
above its limit, then trades down to $42.50, so the model fills it at $42.72. Because the fill
happened intraday, the entry bar cannot credit a target, and the stop is not reached. At the
close, five slots are in use: Fir, Alder, Birch, Dogwood, and Cedar. Hazel then signals at $51.80
and passes every filter, but the halted Fir still holds a slot, so Hazel gets no order. Equity is
$100,502.82, and holdings are 45.6% of it, the highest exposure so far.

What the ledger can and cannot tell you
The +0.74% change over seven sessions is evidence of nothing about Atlas-20's merit. It comes
from four closed trades and three open ones, invented to exercise the rules. What the ledger
does show is structural. Exposure peaked at 45.6% in this supplied path. Entry caps constrain
orders at their limits; subsequent mark changes can move holdings above those percentages.
Slots, not cash, rationed the opportunities: Dogwood at decision close o and Hazel at decision
close 3 were eligible and turned away. The conventions also matter, though not in one
direction. Stop-first turned Birch's ambiguous bar into - $241 instead of +$467. The
system-design-answers-26.png:
participation cap shrank that same losing trade from 138 to 118 shares, which reduced its loss
by $40. The touch rule kept Cedar out at $41.20, which changed which candidates later
received slots; the supplied bars cannot price that alternative path. Conservative here means
not assuming an unproven favorable fill, not always lowering the result.
The ledger also keeps the decisions that never became trades. Elm and Ginkgo were ineligible,
Cedar did not fill, Dogwood and Hazel found no free slot, and Ginkgo's record was incomplete.
Testing, discussed in the earlier evidence chapter, needs exactly this full opportunity set. A
researcher who keeps only the trades cannot ask whether the ranking rule, the slot limit, or the
earnings window is doing useful work. Answering those questions takes many more
opportunities than this scenario provides, held-out data, and realistic costs. The case studies in
the last chapter return to such records.
A regime filter would be version 1.1
A regime filter restricts trading according to a defined market state. Atlas-20 v1.0 has none.
Adding one creates a new version that needs its own data contract. A complete specification
might read: "No new entries at a decision close unless the fictional benchmark's completed
close exceeds the simple average of its previous 50 completed closes. Existing positions are
unaffected. If the benchmark bar is missing, no new entries." That sentence names the series,
the lookback, the timestamp, what the filter blocks, and its missing-data rule. It is still a
hypothesis, not an improvement. A filter can skip losing periods and also miss rebounds. If its
definition is repeatedly altered to fit the same history, the search grows while the final system
appears more careful.
The separate fictional figure contrasts two predetermined exposure schedules over an invented
price path. The switching path holds 101 in cash for steps 4-7 and reenters at an index of 92, so
its later values equal 101 x index ÷ 92. The figure shows the consequences of exposure timing,
not evidence that any filter can identify those dates. In a real test, every switch must follow
information available at the time, and cash returns and costs must be included. Measuring only
the invested periods would hide the opportunity cost of sitting in cash.

Specify when to pause and how to improve
A monitoring plan compares observed behavior with the specification: signal counts, data
completeness, exposure, costs, and differences between modeled and actual fills. Atlas-20
separates operational triggers from performance triggers. Fir's missing bar in session 3 fired an
operational trigger. The right response is to confirm the halt and the data feed, not to change a
parameter. The scenario's largest decline from an equity peak, from $100,502.82 to
$100,188.02, is about 0.31%, far from the 8% performance trigger. Even a breached trigger
only starts a review; a losing week is not proof that the hypothesis has failed.
Any change to the rule sheet, whether a new ranking, a different cap, or a regime filter,
becomes a new version with its own record. Bailey and coauthors explain why this matters. The
chance of a false discovery rises with the number of configurations tried on the same data, and
published backtests rarely report how many trials were run. Keep every version and the reason
for it, evaluate on data not used to choose the change, and compare with simpler alternatives. A
complete system is valuable because it exposes every decision to scrutiny. It becomes credible
only through honest evidence, feasible execution, and a risk policy suited to its uncertainty.
Atlas-20 still needs its own empirical test
The research appendix gives supportive momentum evidence and adverse rule-selection
evidence under other specifications. Atlas-20's thresholds, allocation and fills are original
teaching choices. The cash reconciliation proves that the scenario's accounting works; it is not a
held-out real-stock trial or an estimate of its profitability.

A WORKED EXAMPLE
Two limits disagree
At decision close 0, equity is $100,000.00 and the risk allowance is 250 shares for every
candidate. Alder's $32.27 limit allows 309 shares under the 10% notional cap, so risk binds at
250 shares: $8,067.50 of notional and a 1R of $500. Birch's $72.46 limit allows only 138
shares, so notional binds. Its planned risk is $276, but after the partial fill of 118 shares its
frozen 1R is $236. The qualifying signal does not override the tighter limit, and the
denominator follows the shares actually filled.

Rerank decision close o by liquidity
Keep every v1.0 rule except the ranking: rank eligible candidates by 20-session mean dollar

The eligible set is unchanged: Alder, Birch, Cedar, and Dogwood. Ranked by dollar volume, the order

Dogwood: L = floor(1.01 x 61.20) = $61.81. The allowances are 250 shares for risk, floor(10,000 ÷
